newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Amgen optimistic on key drugs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Amgen optimistic on key drugs.

text.p: Amgen Inc Chief Executive Officer Gordon Binder said Friday he expects the strong sales growth rate of the company's two key drugs, Epogen and Neupogen, to slow, but only slightly.
"We are anticipating the growth rate will be less, but not that much less," Binder told Reuters in an interview.
In the 1996 fourth quarter, sales of Epogen rose 22 percent and sales of Neupogen were up 10 percent. The company attributed the growth to "focused marketing initiatives and additional indications."
Epogen boosts red blood cell count. Neupogen does the same for white blood cell count.
Going forward, Binder said he expects other "small things" -- such as aggressive marketing and more favorable reimbursement policies -- to add up to continued strong growth in sales of the two drugs.
He said Epogen sales should benefit from changes in Medicare policies for reimbursing dialysis patients.
Binder said doctors have been discouraged from prescribing too much Epogen for fear of raising a patient's red blood cell count above the point at which Medicare pays for dialysis.
Doctors should have more leeway to give larger doses under new rules that measure red blood cell count on a three-month moving average rather than month to month, he said.
"Doctors will be willing to take them higher in the allowed range," he said.
Sustained sales growth for Neupogen partly reflects more focused marketing aimed at educating doctors about the drug's benefits, Binder said.
"There are quite a few patients who could benefit from Neupogen who are not currently using it," he said.

Marketing efforts will increasingly highlight the cost benefits of Neupogen, which allieviates some of the side effects of chemotherapy, resulting in shorter hospital stays and reduced use of antibiotics, he said.
Amgen's aggressive marketing of the two drugs coincides with efforts to launch new drugs that will allow the company to sustain its strong growth rate.
Binder said he expects the Food and Drug Administration to approve its Infergen drug for Hepatitis C later this year.
He said he was hopeful the FDA would approve Amgen's stem cell factor (SCF) in 1998.
Binder said the company's decision to repurchase up to $450 million of its stock in 1997 was based on internal investment considerations.
"We've been repurchasing Amgen shares all along," he said. "We generate a lot of cash and haven't found an investment that we like better."
Amgen announced the repurchase plan Thursday, when it reported a 23 percent increase in 1996 fourth quarter earnings.
